limits: This is a retrospective official account rather than the complete 1854 report.
It does not resolve who authored particular examinations, thresholds, curricula, or exceptions.
observed_propositions: The official history characterizes open competition and merit promotion as reforms against patronage.
The source supports an authentic anti-corruption origin; it does not establish that every later merit instrument is neutral or equivalent.
sources.passage_locator: Passage describing the 1854 Northcote–Trevelyan recommendations for open competitive examination, recruitment and promotion on merit, and removal of patronage and purchase.
sources.title: Timeless values in an age of change

limits: The statute concerns the U.S. federal civil service and does not itself govern contemporary private hiring.
It does not prove that the examinations captured every valuable capacity or eliminated all discretion.
observed_propositions: The Act joined competitive examination to probation and durable administrative recordkeeping.
The anti-patronage reform placed operational burdens on the selecting institution rather than treating a score as a self-sufficient decision.
sources.passage_locator: Act provisions concerning competitive practical examinations, grade-based appointments, probation, and written records of appointments, rejections, transfers, resignations, removals, and exceptions.
sources.title: Pendleton Act (1883)

limits: The source is a primary management text, not an empirical validation of Taylorism’s claims.
The text does not establish contemporary prevalence or employer-specific causation.
observed_propositions: Scientific management places job decomposition, method, selection, training, and planning under management authority.
The primary text supports a managerial-control genealogy without proving a direct technical lineage to every modern HR instrument.
sources.passage_locator: Taylor’s principles assigning management responsibility for developing the science of work and scientifically selecting, training, and developing workers.
sources.title: The Principles of Scientific Management

limits: The text is a historical programmatic claim, not proof that its experiments validly predicted all job performance.
It cannot support universal claims about industrial psychology or modern assessment practice.
observed_propositions: Münsterberg explicitly framed industrial psychology as matching persons to management-defined economic work.
The text supports the shift from public anti-patronage merit toward managerial fit and output.
sources.passage_locator: Chapters framing vocational selection around mental qualities that best fit economic work and around securing the greatest useful output.
sources.title: Psychology and Industrial Efficiency

limits: The museum record is a historical overview, not a complete validation archive.
It does not establish a single uninterrupted lineage to present-day employment tests.
observed_propositions: More than 1.7 million soldiers took Army intelligence tests during World War I.
The institutional use of the score exceeded contemporary certainty about construct and performance relation.
sources.passage_locator: Object history describing Army Alpha’s scale, tested content, and contemporary uncertainty about what the tests measured and how scores related to military performance.
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution / National Museum of American History
sources.title: Group Examination Alpha

limits: Historical alternative administration should not be equated with modern disability accommodation.
The record does not establish fairness across language, culture, race, or disability groups.
observed_propositions: The wartime classification system altered administration for heterogeneous recruits while preserving mass throughput.
Different administration did not itself resolve the validity, threshold, or downstream error-distribution questions.
sources.passage_locator: Object history describing a nonverbal group test for recruits who could not read English and its pantomimed administration.
sources.title: Group Examination Beta

limits: A historical forerunner is not proof of construct identity with current personality assessments.
The source does not establish the validity or fairness of later instruments.
observed_propositions: The inventory represents an early attempt to classify psychological risk through standardized self-report.
The instrument was not mass operational during the war but became a forerunner of later personality inventories.
sources.passage_locator: Object history describing Woodworth’s yes/no inventory for identifying recruits thought susceptible to shell shock, its late arrival, and its later influence.
sources.title: Personal Data Sheet

limits: The episode cannot be generalized to every test or every current practitioner.
The source supports a historical misuse boundary, not a universal indictment of measurement.
observed_propositions: Scores acquired social and political meaning beyond a settled operational-performance construct.
The history demonstrates the consequence of classification authority outrunning valid inference.
sources.passage_locator: Collection history describing Brigham’s use of Army-test data for racial and immigration claims and his later rejection of aspects of his own analysis.
sources.title: A Study of American Intelligence

limits: The guidelines define a professional method; they do not establish that every assessment center is valid or unbiased.
They do not establish the contents of any employer-specific battery not preserved in the source record.
observed_propositions: A genuine assessment center requires behavioral simulation and multiple evidentiary components.
A battery composed only of written or computerized tests is not an assessment center under the professional guidelines.
sources.passage_locator: Definition and essential elements: job analysis, behavioral constructs, multiple components, job-related simulations, overt constructed responses, multiple trained assessors, and the exclusion of test-only batteries from the assessment-center label.
sources.title: Guidelines and Ethical Considerations for Assessment Center Operations
